The National Universities Commission, in partnership with EyeCity Africa, has inaugurated the Higher Education Innovation Working Group to strengthen entrepreneurship education, improve graduate employability and promote research commercialisation in Nigerian higher education institutions. The Working Group will bring together universities, government agencies, private sector organisations and development partners to provide policy advice, mobilise resources and technical expertise, and strengthen collaboration between higher education institutions and industry. The virtual inauguration, held on Wednes day, followed a stakeholder roundtable on entrepreneurship and innovation jointly organised by NUC and EyeCity Africa in Abuja on November 18, 2025. One of the key outcomes of the roundtable was an agreement among participants to establish a working group that would sustain collaboration and support the implementation of recommendations from the engagement. Speaking through the Director of Skills Development and Entrepreneurship, Dr Esther Mmeka, the NUC Executive Secretary, Prof. Abdullahi Ribadu, said the initiative was part of efforts to ensure that research and innovations from Nigerian universities produced practical benefits for students and the wider economy. He said the commission had made progress in integrating entrepreneurship education into university curricula and encouraging institutions to establish structures that support innovation and enterprise development. “Our concern now is how these efforts can produce greater benefits for students, researchers and the wider economy,” he said. Ribadu noted that the challenge was to ensure that knowledge and innovations emerging from universities found practical applications in society. Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. The inauguration also followed the publication of a joint NUC and EyeCity Africa research report in 2026, titled Innovation and Entrepreneurship Landscape within Higher Education Institutions in Nigeria. The research examined entrepreneurship education, innovation hubs, research commercialisation and institutional partnerships, drawing on experiences from institutions across Nigeria’s six geopolitical zones. Its findings showed that Nigerian universities had made progress in establishing structures to support entrepreneurship and innovation, but gaps remained in research commercialisation, industry partnerships, institutional support and access to finance. Mr Omotayo Abraham, Associate Director at EyeCity Africa, said the Working Group was established to sustain the collaboration that began at the 2025 stakeholder roundtable and take forward recommendations from the engagement and subsequent research. Abraham disclosed that EyeCity Africa had trained more than 160 higher education institutions across the continent and engaged over 230 through its learning sessions. The organisation also convenes an active community of nearly 90 higher education institutions working on innovation and entrepreneurship. He encouraged development partners and private sector organisations to contribute their expertise, funding, staff time and institutional networks to initiatives developed through the Working Group. The Group has 10 inaugural member institutions: NUC, EyeCity Africa, the British Council, the Federal Ministry of Education, the National Commission for Colleges of Education, the Nigeria Employers’ Consultative Association, Seed Builders Innovation Hub, Nasarawa State University, Keffi, the African University of Science and Technology, and Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria. NUC and EyeCity Africa will co-chair the Working Group, with EyeCity Africa also serving as its Secretariat. Speaking during the inauguration, the Deputy Vice-Chancellor of Covenant University, Prof. Lanre Amodu, called for stronger collaboration between universities and industry, saying both sides should recognise their distinct roles in preparing graduates for the labour market. “Universities cannot become the same as industry because, of course, industries are solving real-time problems and innovating as they go. Universities have to do with knowledge creation,” he said. Amodu said industry should provide practical materials that universities could incorporate into teaching and curriculum development. “The industry must be willing to supply case studies, data and skills that can be converted into learning points and curriculum building in schools,” he said. He added that such collaboration would help students become familiar with industry technology and the problems they would be expected to solve after graduation. “By that, the students and graduates produced on the platform of the universities are already industry-ready, and this is facilitated by all the partners that are involved,” he said. Presenting the Working Group’s mandate and governance arrangements, Ugwueke identified policy and institutional advice, entrepreneurship and innovation, workforce development, and partnership mobilisation as its principal areas of focus. He explained that members would work together to identify priorities, develop programmes and proposals, mobilise technical and financial support, and monitor progress on agreed initiatives. Ugwueke also confirmed that the Secretariat would coordinate the first formal meeting of the Working Group within two weeks of the inauguration. The meeting will allow members to review the Operational Framework, agree on initial priorities, identify workstream leads and develop a work plan.
